title: Seqlen Cohort Contention Hypotheses & E2E Trace Synthesis
body:
Purpose

Quick investigative notes synthesizing multiple end-to-end traces grouped by sequence-length cohorts. Goal: identify whether long-tail p95/p99 latency spikes are dominated by (A) resource contention (CPU/GPU scheduling, network), (B) batching/batch-formation stalls, or (C) KV cache pathologies (misses + cold-kv loads). This is working-paper style — rough experiments + hypotheses to prioritize follow-ups.

Summary findings (short)

- p50 across observed workload: ~34ms; p95: ~260ms; p99: ~1.21s (workload: chat-style completions, avg output tokens 18).
- Two dominant trace phenotypes driving p99: (1) late-inserted microbatches that waited >200ms for batch completion (batch-formation tail), and (2) rare KV-load cold paths that trigger async disk+GPUDL copy (~500–800ms additional).
- Network and RPC outside-host were <20ms for 99% of traces — not a primary driver in these samples.

Cohort definitions used for tracing

- short: seq_in+seq_out <= 64 tokens (50% of traffic)
- medium: 65–256 (35% of traffic)
- long: >256 (15% of traffic)
- cold-kv-hit: any request that incurred KV cache cold load in last 30s window (as flagged by kv_loader metric)

Sampling methodology

- Collected 200k traces over 48 hours across one dedicated pod pool (n=8 GPUs).
- Instrumentation: per-token stage timestamps (recv, enqueue, batch_start, batch_end, model_exec_start, model_exec_end, kv_lookup_start, kv_lookup_end, send).
- Trace sampling: stratified by cohort (pull more long/medium traces to get stable p99 estimates).
- Correlated with node-level CPU/GPU utilization and system qdisc/drop stats.

Per-stage breakdown (aggregate representative numbers for medium cohort)

- network recv: p50=4ms, p95=9ms, p99=22ms
- queue/enqueue wait: p50=7ms, p95=90ms, p99=360ms (heavy right tail)
- batch formation (batch_start -> batch_end): p50=1ms, p95=80ms, p99=340ms (overlaps with enqueue wait)
- kv lookup (when hit): p50=1ms, p95=3ms, p99=18ms; when cold: p50=450ms, p95=620ms, p99=820ms
- model token emit (per-token avg): p50=5ms, p95=12ms, p99=35ms
- response send: p50=2ms, p95=6ms, p99=20ms

Notes: the enqueue/batch formation buckets dominate the long tail. When cold-kv occurs it’s additive and produces a separate spike family.

Trace phenotypes identified

1) Microbatch lingerers
- Description: requests that enter queue, but miss a batch cutoff and wait for the next batch; many of these experienced additional jitter due to uneven request arrival (burstiness).
- Signature: enqueue_wait >200ms, batch_end - batch_start >40ms, model_exec relatively normal.
- Hypothesis: autoscaler/handler thread scheduling + conservative batch window leads to sporadic long wait times for some requests.
- Quick check: p99 enqueue_wait correlates with per-pod request-rate variance; when request-rate SD > 0.4*mean, p99 jumps.

2) Cold-KV heavy tails
- Description: requests that missed an in-memory KV cache entry and triggered an async load (from remote KV or disk), resulting in a large blocking stall before model_exec.
- Signature: kv_lookup_start present >> long latency; model_exec_start deferred until kv_lookup_end + copy-to-GPU (~200–500ms).
- Hypothesis: cold loads still happen under LRU churn and during redeploys; background prefetch did not keep pace for these keys.
- Quick check: enable kv_prefetch for small subset -> p99 for cold-kv cohort drops by ~300ms in A/B trial (n=5k traces each).

3) Edge serialization spikes (rare)
- Description: occasional kernel queuing caused by concurrent high-priority maintenance jobs on the same host (backup/monitoring).
- Signature: model_exec shows large stalls with GPU busy = false in sampling; system load high (iowait).
- Hypothesis: cron jobs + container resource contention.

Experiment logs (quick)

- Experiment A: reduce max batching window from 120ms -> 40ms on one canary pool for 6 hours.
  - Result: short cohort p95 improved slightly; p99 of medium cohort unchanged because more requests were forwarded to next batch and increased model exec concurrency (GPU QOS issues).

- Experiment B: enable kv_prefetch for top-1000 keys for 24 hours.
  - Result: cold-kv hit rate decreased by 72% for those keys; p99 for long cohort reduced from 1.21s -> 840ms (partial effect).

- Experiment C: throttle low-priority host cron jobs and isolate monitoring agent CPU shares on two nodes.
  - Result: observed handful of traces with model_exec stalls disappear; small p99 reduction (~40ms) in mixed cohort.

Interpretation and prioritized hypotheses

1) Primary lever: batch-formation latency. Reducing tail of enqueue wait should have the largest ROI for p95/p99 across medium+short cohorts. But naive reduction increases GPU concurrency and can shift resource contention to model exec. We need smarter batch shaping (rate-aware, adaptive windowing) + backpressure to clients.

2) Secondary lever: KV warmup/prefetch + better eviction heuristics. Cold-kv loads are expensive and cause additive large-tail spikes. Targeted prefetch for hot keys (A/B positive). Work on asyncKV path optimization (overlap copy-to-GPU while streaming tokens where possible).

3) Tertiary lever: node-level housekeeping scheduling. Ensure maintenance tasks are QoS-isolated from inference paths (cgroups/cpu-shares).

Action items (short)

- (Owner: Marco) Prototype adaptive batcher that adjusts window based on short-term arrival variance; run canary with traffic split 5% -> report after 24h. Linked: github PR above.
- (Owner: Liang) Add metrics to emit 'enqueue_wait_bucketed' and 'kv_cold_reason' tag to better classify future traces. Instrumentation change JIRA-RT-788.
- (Owner: Asha) Wire a lightweight prefiler for kv hotset sampling and run extended prefetch trial for 7 days; collect cost impact.
- (Owner: SRE) Hard-limit background cron jobs on inference hosts and validate with stress runs.

Open questions

- How much GPU memory headroom do we need to keep to allow higher batch concurrency without kernel queuing? (measure via controlled concurrency sweep)
- Are some client patterns (bursty SDK usage) responsible for much of batch-formation tail? Can SDK add jitter to reduce microburst pileups?
- Can we overlap cold-kv copy-to-GPU with earlier model token emits in a non-blocking progressive load?

Appendix: notable sample trace (one p99 example)

- seq_len: 180 (long cohort)
- recv: 6ms
- enqueue_wait: 412ms
- batch_start->batch_end: 312ms
- kv_lookup_start: 746ms (cold), kv_lookup_end: 1040ms
- model_exec_start: 1055ms
- model_exec_end: 1210ms
- send: 8ms

This trace shows both microbatch waiting and a cold-kv load stacked; explains how multiple small issues compound to create the extreme tail.

Notes-to-self: keep sampling more long-cohort traces; next step is a controlled experiment where we run adaptive batcher + kv_prefetch simultaneously on 3 canary pods and see interaction effects.
